items.heading: Heading
items.paragraph:
Ever know an individual who tried to fight every battle? Maybe you’re thinking of someone in your office right now. You may even be thinking of yourself!

As a woman, there are a few strategic principles to staying in it for the long haul and making your career go the distance when others before you have flamed out.

Become a Go-To Team Player

The first is, become a go-to team member. Remember the previous lesson about being your authentic self? Don’t wait for recognition or a promotion to become an ideal team player. As a coach, Pat intentionally looked for players who wanted the ball—those who had declared themselves competitors and felt confident enough in their skills to request the ball when the game was on the line. Their team knew they could count on them to perform so they became the go-to. 

This takes intentionality and sometimes going above and beyond in strategic areas. The key word is strategic. Learn how to best add value to your team without automatically accepting every assignment that comes your way.

items.heading: Heading
items.paragraph: You can’t fight every battle. You just cannot. When it comes to women in the workplace overall, and your career specifically, know which battles to fight and which to leave alone. Grow your long-term perspective. This has several advantages as you progress as a female leader.

items.title: Strategic Decision-Making
items.description: Knowing when to pick your battles involves assessing the importance of an issue, understanding the potential impact on your career, and considering the long-term consequences of engaging in a particular issue.

items.title: Preserving Energy and Focus
items.description: Engaging in every battle can be exhausting and detract from your overall focus and productivity. Knowing when to pick your battles allows you to preserve your energy for the issues that truly matter.

items.title: Demonstrating Emotional Intelligence
items.description: Emotional intelligence plays a big role in workplace dynamics. Choosing battles requires recognizing and managing emotions effectively, leading to more constructive interactions between you and your peers.

items.title: Distinguishing Between Major and Minor Issues
items.description: Not every workplace issue requires the same level of your attention. Period. Major issues that align with your core values or significantly impact your work should be prioritized.

items.title: Assessing the Long-Term Impact
items.description: Consider the long-term impact of a potential conflict. Will the issue at hand have lasting consequences on your career, relationships, or the overall work environment?

items.title: Evaluating Personal Investment
items.description: If the matter directly affects your responsibilities, well-being, or professional growth, it may be worth addressing. However, for issues that are more peripheral to your role, choosing to step back might be the wiser option.

items.heading: Deep Dive: Guardrails for Burnout
items.paragraph: When we show up to the present moment with all of our senses, we invite the world to fill us with joy. The pains of the past are behind us. The future has yet to unfold. But the now is full of beauty simply waiting for our attention.

When it comes to being “in it for the long haul,” one classic challenge female leaders face is a greater susceptibility to burnout. Burnout can look quite different for each individual, and a lot of it can be prevented on the front end with a little intentionality. First, you want to stop and think about your overall career goals and where your career “guardrails” are, what you will and won’t do. This is important, because it’s easy to eagerly accept long hours, salary changes, or a change in commute in the wake of an exciting new promotion. But without an honest assessment of your personal guardrails, women often find themselves landing squarely in the burnout zone. Don’t let this be you!

Your guardrails may change over the course of your career, and that’s OK! The important thing is to stop and think about where you are now and where you want to be. If, 10 years from now, you’re doing exactly the same thing as you are now, is that OK? What are the “non-negotiables” in your career when it comes to salary, work hours, long weekends, travel, location, commute, flexibility, etc.?

Some things are OK for a season, but you want to make sure you understand where your personal boundaries are as your career progresses.

Because of caregiving duties and other factors we mentioned earlier, women are often more susceptible to burnout than men. The signs are subtle and easy to miss, but if you learn to course-correct before hitting the ditch, you’ll go farther and be able to perform better in your career.
